To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Immunostaining for the mismatch repair (MMRs) proteins MLH1 and MSH2 is a reliable tool for detecting HNPCC tumors.

1) MSI-high tumors are characterized by immunohistochemical losses of MLH1 (in 48% of cases), MSH2 (36%), and MSH6 (36%) and that 2) immunohistochemical staining for these MMR proteins has a sensitivity of 93% and a specificity 100% for identifying MMR-defective tumors.
immunostaining for MMR proteins MLHI, MSH2 and MSH6 has a sensitivity of 100% and a specificity 100% in the detection of MMR-deficient colorectal tumors.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of novel diagnostic methods for the detection of HNPCC and other cancers caused by MMR gene mutations.
the identification and characterization of novel biomarkers for cancer.
the molecular mechanisms underlying the development of colorectal cancer in HNPCC patients and how the genetic defect can be used for early cancer detection.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
MSI and MSH2/MLH1 immunostaining should be performed in all suspected HNPCC cases.
MMR protein immunohistochemistry has a high sensitivity and specificity for the diagnosis of HNPCC.

the presence of microsatellite instability is a prerequisite for HNPCC diagnosis, but that MMR protein immunohistochemistry may be used to confirm the presence of a MMR defect in the case of a MSI-positive tumor.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
MSI and MSH6 immunostaining are the most sensitive and specific methods available for identifying HNPCC-associated tumors.

MSI and MSH2/MLH1 immunostaining should be performed in every patient suspected of having HNCC, and that the combination of MSI analysis and MSH2 and/or MLH1 immunostainings are sufficient in most cases.

immunostaining for MMR proteins is a useful supplement in HNPCC analysis, especially in patients without known germ-line mutations, but that MSI analysis is still necessary for the detection of tumors without MMR protein loss.
The main takeaway from our work is that
MMR immunohistochemistry is an important tool for the diagnosis of Lynch syndrome.
immunostaining for MMR proteins is a useful adjunct to MSI analysis in clinical HNPCCC diagnosis.
MMR protein immunohistochemistry is a useful tool in HNPCC diagnostics, but MSI should be included in the analysis.
